source.title_on_document: Augmenting Minds or Automating Skills? The Differential Role of Human Capital in Generative AI's Impact on Creative Tasks

supplement.where: Online Appendices A to F; data, code, output, and materials at https://osf.io/ynhtu/?view_only=31642f7caac74082940eb1153d4e9e55 (p. 1, Author Note; p. 16, footnote 1)
supplement.holds: Survey measures and rating criteria (Appendices A, C), lyric-task materials (Appendix B), supplementary analyses including the embedding-similarity analyses and omnibus models (Appendices D and E), and simple-slope figures for usefulness and overall impression (Appendix F). The embedding-similarity statistics for Experiment 1 are not printed in the main text.

paper_design_summary: Two randomized experiments in China assigned participants to write with a GPT-4 chat interface or without AI. In Experiment 1 (lab, 162 participants) each person wrote one flash fiction of under 500 Chinese characters; in Experiment 2 (online, one week) participants wrote song lyrics to a supplied melody, and 329 lyrics from 299 participants were rated and recorded as songs. Online rater panels scored novelty, usefulness, and overall impression, and the paper also reports embedding similarity of outputs by condition; the main focus is moderation of the AI effect by education, IQ, and domain expertise.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of a GPT-4 chat tool to write the flash fiction versus writing without AI assistance
assignment.quote: Second, they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: one group used generative AI (GPT-4) to compose a flash-fiction of under 500 Chinese characters, while the other group completed the task without AI assistance.
assignment.locator: p. 16, Experiment 1, Samples and Procedures; p. 48, Figure 1

arms.name: AI group
arms.description: Wrote the flash fiction with a dialogue-based GPT-4 interface; received basic fiction-writing instructions plus guidance on prompt crafting

arms.name: No-AI group
arms.description: Wrote the flash fiction without AI; received basic fiction-writing instructions

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions reported; 162 individuals participated and all regressions use 162 observations (Table 2). Arm sizes are not reported. Two raters (not participants) were excluded for failed attention checks.
participants.who: People with an interest in story creation recruited via social media and online interest groups: 101 college students, the rest working in sectors such as technology and education; mean age 26.27, 68.52 percent female, 95.06 percent with at least a bachelor's degree
participants.quote: 162 individuals participated in the first experiment, each compensated 30 CNY.
participants.locator: p. 16, Experiment 1, Samples and Procedures; p. 41, Table 2 (Observations = 162)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via OpenAI API, in a dialogue-based interface built by the authors
ai_tool.how_used: Participants chatted freely with the tool while writing (example interface in Figure 3); the AI group received extra guidance on effective prompt crafting.

task.description: Write one flash fiction of under 500 Chinese characters in a behavioral lab
task.duration: not stated (single lab session; described as a constrained timeframe, p. 22)

outcomes.name: Novelty of the story (rater panel)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual assessment by an online panel of public raters, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .90-.91; about 43.87 raters per story (SD 1.77). Full-sample mean 4.879, SD 1.036 (Table 1, not by arm). OLS with robust SEs controlling for education, IQ, specific human capital, age, gender, openness, AI use frequency, purpose for experiment, mind perception, and the raters' AI identification ratio. Models 2a, 2b, and 3 add interaction terms and give AI Use coefficients of 0.382, 0.361, and 0.386.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.403 (robust SE 0.19), p = .035; N = 162; R-squared 0.178 (Table 2, Model 1, Novelty)

outcomes.name: Usefulness of the story (rater panel)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Degree to which the story provoked thought and conveyed meaningful insights; online public rater panel, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .87-.89. Full-sample mean 4.799, SD 0.940 (Table 1). Same OLS controls as S1-O1. Models 2a, 2b, 3 AI Use coefficients 0.339, 0.329, 0.321.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.352 (robust SE 0.16), p = .032; N = 162; R-squared 0.263 (Table 2, Model 1, Usefulness)

outcomes.name: Overall impression / overall enjoyment of the story (rater panel)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall enjoyment rating, included 'to assess the quality of each story' (p. 17); online public rater panel, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .89-.91. Full-sample mean 4.912, SD 0.918 (Table 1). Same OLS controls as S1-O1. Models 2a, 2b, 3 AI Use coefficients 0.357, 0.340, 0.349. Coded 'other' (liking/quality), not a creativity rating; could alternatively be read as usefulness (quality).

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.370 (robust SE 0.15), p = .015; N = 162; R-squared 0.315 (Table 2, Model 1, Overall Impression)

outcomes.name: Similarity of stories (text embeddings)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Supplementary analysis using 'textual analysis techniques (embedding)'; no statistics printed in the main text; details referred to online Appendix D.

contrasts.reported: 'our findings showed no significant increase in similarity among AI-assisted outputs compared to those created independently' (no numbers printed)

diversity_detail.metric: Embedding-based similarity (exact metric not stated in main text)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: not stated (significance test referred to; method not described in main text)
diversity_detail.notes: Unit set to output by analogy with Experiment 2's regression coefficients; the main text does not state the unit. Statistics likely in online Appendix D, not in this PDF. Sign: the paper reports similarity, so higher similarity = lower diversity.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing lyrics with a GPT-4 chat tool versus without AI support
assignment.quote: After registration and an online IQ test (Nstart = 685), participants were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted group or a control group that composed lyrics without AI support.
assignment.locator: p. 23, Experiment 2, Sample and Procedures; p. 49, Figure 2

arms.name: AI-assisted group
arms.description: Wrote lyrics for an assigned song demo with the GPT-4 chat interface over one week; received lyric-writing instructions plus guidance on using generative AI

arms.name: Control group (no AI)
arms.description: Wrote lyrics for an assigned song demo without AI support over one week; received lyric-writing instructions

participants.exclusions: Nstart = 685 registered and took the IQ test before assignment; Ninformation = 611 after the information session; Nsubmission = 348 submitted lyrics; 'dropout rate of 43.04%' at the lyrics-creation stage. Of the submissions, 329 works from 299 participants were deemed suitable for recording and analyzed; 289 participants (96.66 percent) wrote one song, so some contributed several works. Attrition by arm is not reported. The 685 is the count at registration immediately before random assignment; the text does not state that all 685 were assigned.
participants.who: Recruited from universities, companies, and online music platforms, ranging from lyric novices to people with publication experience; final sample mean age 24.10, 63.88 percent female, 93.31 percent with a bachelor's degree or higher
participants.country: not stated (compensation in CNY; authors at Chinese universities)
participants.quote: Among the submissions, 329 works from 299 participants were deemed suitable for song recording by professional producers and singers.
participants.locator: p. 23-24, Experiment 2, Sample and Procedures; pp. 43-44, Tables 4-5 (Observations = 329)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via OpenAI API, in a dialogue-based interface built by the authors
ai_tool.how_used: Free chat use during a one-week online lyric-writing task; the AI group received extra guidance on using generative AI.

task.description: Write Chinese song lyrics for an assigned demo (accompaniment plus vocal melody, with simplified score and suggested word counts); lyrics were then sung by trained choir members and produced into songs
task.duration: one week, at own pace, online

outcomes.name: Novelty of lyrics (rated without music)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Online rater panel rated lyrics alone on originality and unique expression; 10-point scale, ICC2 = .35-.52; about 5.12 raters per lyric (SD 0.71). Full-sample mean 5.012, SD 1.015 (Table 3). OLS with robust SEs (not clustered by participant), demo fixed effects, and the same controls as Experiment 1.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.087 (robust SE 0.11), not significant; N = 329 works; R-squared 0.249 (Table 4, col. 2, Novelty_L)

outcomes.name: Usefulness (emotional expression) of lyrics (rated without music)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Extent to which the emotional content resonates with the audience; lyrics-only rater panel, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .26-.41. Full-sample mean 5.374, SD 0.950 (Table 3). Same specification as S2-O1.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.079 (robust SE 0.11), not significant; N = 329; R-squared 0.216 (Table 4, col. 4, Usefulness_L)

outcomes.name: Overall impression of lyrics (rated without music)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 'Overall quality and impact of the lyrics themselves'; lyrics-only rater panel, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .42-.59. Full-sample mean 5.366, SD 1.026 (Table 3). Same specification as S2-O1. Coded 'other' (overall quality), not a creativity rating.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.097 (robust SE 0.12), not significant; N = 329; R-squared 0.246 (Table 4, col. 6, Overall Impression_L)

outcomes.name: Novelty of the recorded song
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Lyrics were sung by trained university choir members and produced into songs; a separate online panel rated the songs, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .85-.87; about 28.33 raters per song (SD 1.61). Full-sample mean 4.836, SD 0.744 (Table 3). OLS with robust SEs, demo fixed effects, same controls.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.133 (robust SE 0.07), p = .061; N = 329; R-squared 0.446 (Table 5, col. 2, Novelty_S); the paper says the effect 'did not reach statistical significance'

outcomes.name: Usefulness (emotional appeal) of the recorded song
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Song rater panel, 10-point scale, ICC2 = .78-.81. Full-sample mean 5.143, SD 0.636 (Table 3). Same specification as S2-O4.

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.108 (robust SE 0.06), p = .075; N = 329; R-squared 0.454 (Table 5, col. 4, Usefulness_S); not statistically significant per the paper

outcomes.name: Overall impression (listener liking) of the recorded song
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Overall impression of the songs 'based on their liking as listeners'; song rater panel, ICC2 = .83-.85. Full-sample mean 4.944, SD 0.681 (Table 3). Same specification as S2-O4. Coded 'other' (liking).

contrasts.reported: AI Use b = 0.087 (robust SE 0.06), not significant; N = 329; R-squared 0.512 (Table 5, col. 6, Overall Impression_S)

outcomes.name: Similarity of lyrics (text embeddings)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Supplementary analysis with 'textual analysis techniques (embedding)'; two variants, cosine similarity and L2 distance. Regression coefficients and p-values printed without standard errors; details referred to online appendices.

contrasts.reported: Increased similarity among AI-assisted outputs: Cosine b = 0.014, p = .008; L2 distance b = -0.014, p = .007 (sign reversed for diversity: AI arm less diverse)

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity and L2 distance between text embeddings
diversity_detail.computed_over: not stated (coefficients suggest a per-output similarity score regressed on AI use, but the main text does not say which outputs are compared)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Regression coefficient with p-value; method of SE not stated in main text
diversity_detail.notes: Paper reports similarity; direction coded for diversity (treatment_lower = AI outputs more similar). Unit and n not stated in the main text.

company_involvement.description: All authors at Tsinghua University and Wuhan University of Technology; GPT-4 accessed through OpenAI's API, no company role stated.

eligibility.reason: Both experiments randomly assign individuals to a GPT-4 chat tool versus no AI on a creative writing task (pp. 16, 23). Experiment 1 analyzes 162 people (p. 16; Table 2); Experiment 2 analyzes 299 people (329 works) after heavy attrition from 685 registrants (pp. 23-24). Outcomes are rater-scored novelty, usefulness, and overall impression of the outputs plus embedding similarity. Arm sizes are not reported for either experiment, and Experiment 2 lost most of its randomized sample before analysis with no attrition-by-arm information.

one_line_finding: In Experiment 1 (162 people, flash fiction) GPT-4 access raised rated novelty by 0.403 points on a 10-point scale (SE 0.19, p = .035) and usefulness by 0.352 (SE 0.16) (p. 41, Table 2); in Experiment 2 (299 people, 329 lyrics) effects were small and not significant (lyrics novelty 0.087, SE 0.11; song novelty 0.133, SE 0.07, p = .061; pp. 43-44, Tables 4-5), and AI-assisted lyrics were more similar to one another (cosine b = 0.014, p = .008; p. 29).
open_questions: Arm sizes are not reported in either experiment. In Experiment 1, the mean-split analyses of AI-group interaction (Nlow + Nhigh = 111, t(109); p. 21) suggest about 111 AI-arm participants of 162, but the paper does not label that count as the AI arm. In Experiment 2 the corresponding splits sum to 197 (t(195); p. 28). Check the OSF data.

Experiment 2: does 685 equal the number randomized? The paper gives Nstart = 685 in the sentence describing random assignment, then 611, 348, and 299 people. Attrition by arm is not reported, so differential attrition cannot be ruled out.
All models control for the raters' 'AI identification ratio', which is measured after treatment and is likely affected by AI use; no specification without this control is printed in the main text.
Experiment 2 regressions use 329 works from 299 people with robust (not participant-clustered) SEs.
Construct coding of 'overall impression' (enjoyment/liking/overall quality): coded 'other' here; another screener may code it as usefulness (quality) or overall creativity.
Experiment 1 similarity statistics and the embedding method for both experiments are only in the online appendices (OSF), not in this PDF.
notes: PDF page numbers equal the printed page numbers. The main purpose of the paper is moderation of the AI effect by education, IQ, and domain expertise (AI Use x moderator interactions in Tables 2 and 6-8); those interaction estimates are not listed as separate outcomes. Self-reported outcomes (psychological ownership: Exp 1 b = -1.239, p = .001, p. 21; Exp 2 b = -1.124, p = .000, and creative self-efficacy b = 0.284, p = .014, p. 29) are not scored on output and are omitted from the outcome list. Experiment 2 also measured specific human capital (prior lyric publication) and Figure 2 shows professional lyricists and novices crossed with AI/no-AI, but expertise was measured, not assigned.
